  • Field Museum, Chicago museum · 1893 · 41.8662, -87.6170Founded from 1893 World's Columbian Exposition collections. Marshall Field (department stores) funded. 40+ million specimens. Sue the T-Rex ($8.4M, 1997). Indigenous collections: human remains and sacred objects held for decades before NAGPRA compliance. The natural history museum funded by the retail baron.
  • Fondation Louis Vuitton, Paris museum · 48.8808, 2.2647Bernard Arnault (LVMH). Frank Gehry building in the Bois de Boulogne, opened 2014; projected at EUR 100M, it cost nearly eight times that, and LVMH received EUR 518M in tax breaks (Court of Audit, 2018). Houses the group's collection. Arnault also owned the auction house Phillips 1999-2000s. The vertical integration of taste.
  • Frick Collection, New York museum · 1892 · 40.7710, -73.9672Henry Clay Frick: chairman of Carnegie Steel during the Homestead Strike (1892) - hired Pinkerton agents; seven strikers and three Pinkertons were killed. Anarchist Alexander Berkman tried to assassinate Frick; Frick survived and broke the union. The fortune built this Fifth Avenue mansion-museum: Vermeer, Rembrandt, Bellini, Holbein. The Pinkerton budget became the Vermeer budget.
  • Geneva Freeport, Switzerland - Art Storage Tax Haven financial · 46.1881, 6.1262The largest freeport for art: an estimated US$100bn of art (press estimate) and ~1.2 million works (2013) in duty-suspended warehouses. Bought at auction, stored, resold years later without being seen. Art as bearer bonds.
  • Getty Museum / Getty Villa, Los Angeles museum · 34.0780, -118.4741J. Paul Getty - oil fortune (Getty Oil, later Texaco then Chevron). Getty Villa: 44,000 Greek, Roman and Etruscan antiquities. Curator Marion True (1986-2005) was charged in Italy and Greece over looted antiquities; the cases ended without conviction (statute of limitations), and the Getty returned 40 objects to Italy and others to Greece. Endowment ~$9.4bn (2025), the largest of any art institution.
  • Grand Egyptian Museum, Giza museum · 2025-11-01 · 29.9950, 31.1193Billion-dollar museum near the Giza pyramids, inaugurated 1 Nov 2025, holding over 100,000 objects including the Tutankhamun collection moved from the Egyptian Museum in Tahrir, Cairo (~120,000 objects). Access to Egypt's sites and the official narrative run through the antiquities ministry; Zahi Hawass dominated it for decades until 2011.
  • Great Pyramid of Giza, Egypt archaeological · 29.9792, 31.1342An estimated 2.3 million blocks (~6 million tonnes). Built c. 2560 BC. Sides aligned to the cardinal points within a few arcminutes; star-sighting methods that achieve this are documented in the Egyptological literature.
  • Great Ziggurat of Ur, Dhi Qar, Iraq archaeological · 30.9628, 46.1031A massive Sumerian stepped temple-platform to the moon god Nanna, built c. 2100 BC by King Ur-Nammu near modern Nasiriyah; its restored lower facade sits beside a former Iraqi airbase, and it anchors the ancient city of Ur, traditionally linked to the biblical Abraham. Source: Britannica, 'Ziggurat of Ur' / Wikipedia.
  • Great Zimbabwe National Monument, Masvingo archaeological · -20.2709, 30.9332The mortarless dry-stone Great Enclosure - a wall up to 9.6 m high and 250 m long - is the largest ancient structure in sub-Saharan Africa, capital of a trading empire (11th-15th c.) whose African authorship colonial authorities long tried to deny; it gives the modern nation its name. Source: Britannica, 'Great Zimbabwe' / Wikipedia.
  • Guggenheim Museum, New York - Solomon R. Guggenheim Foundation museum · 40.7830, -73.9590Solomon Guggenheim: mining fortune. Peggy Guggenheim's Venice palazzo is still a museum. Guggenheim Bilbao (Frank Gehry) turned a declining industrial city into a destination - the 'Bilbao Effect'. A Guggenheim Helsinki was rejected by Helsinki City Council in 2016 after polls showed most residents opposed.
  • Göbekli Tepe Excavation Site Museum, Urfa museum · 1994 · 37.2231, 38.9222Museum adjacent to world's oldest known temple (pre-12,000 years). Klaus Schmidt excavated 1994-2014 (died 2014). Only 5% excavated. Turkish government controls access and narrative. An archaeological site that rewrites human history - 95% of it deliberately left in the ground.
  • Göbekli Tepe, Turkey archaeological · 37.2231, 38.9222Pre-Pottery Neolithic site occupied c. 9500-8000 BCE (~11,500 years ago), with large circular enclosures of carved T-shaped limestone pillars. Popularly called the 'world's first temple', but no definitive purpose has been established. Schmidt's early idea that it was deliberately backfilled has been revised: the enclosures repeatedly collapsed, were buried by landslides and were rebuilt.
  • Heard Island, Australian External Territory enclave · -53.1000, 73.5133Subantarctic volcanic island, uninhabited; Big Ben (summit Mawson Peak, 2,745 m) holds Australia's only active volcanoes. ANARE ran a station here 1947-55. One of the most remote places on Earth; a World Heritage nature reserve.
  • Hermitage Museum, St. Petersburg museum · 1764 · 59.9398, 30.31463 million items. Founded by Catherine the Great (1764). Winter Palace - seat of Romanov power. Survived revolution, Nazi siege (872 days, 1M dead in Leningrad). The museum that survived the empire that built it, the revolution that overthrew it, and the siege that tried to starve it.
  • House of Wisdom, Baghdad, Iraq archaeological · 1258 · 33.3405, 44.4009Abbasid library and academy in Baghdad, destroyed in the Mongol siege of 1258. Chroniclers record that so many books were thrown into the Tigris that the river was said to run black with ink (chronicle account). No reliable count of its holdings exists.
  • Humboldt Forum, Berlin museum · 2021 · 52.5170, 13.4012The Prussian Cultural Heritage Foundation agreed in 2021-22 to restitute about 530 Benin Bronzes — looted by British forces in 1897 — held in Berlin's Ethnological Museum to Nigeria, a landmark in the global colonial-restitution debate, though roughly a third are to remain on loan in Berlin. Source: Euronews; Staatliche Museen zu Berlin (smb.museum); Artnet.
  • International Spy Museum, Washington D.C. museum · 2002 · 38.8833, -77.0231Founded by Milton Maltz (Malrite Communications), opened 19 July 2002; now an independent non-profit, at L'Enfant Plaza since 2019. Large public collection of espionage artefacts; advisers have included former intelligence directors. The public version of the story, told while the classified one continues.
  • Isabella Stewart Gardner Museum, Boston museum · 1990-03-18 · 42.3382, -71.0992On March 18, 1990, two thieves disguised as police officers spent 81 minutes stealing 13 works - including a Vermeer and Rembrandts - valued at hundreds of millions of dollars: the highest-value museum robbery in history. Unsolved; the museum's $10 million reward stands. Source: FBI; Smithsonian Magazine.
  • KAWS Companion Sculptures - Various Locations obelisk · 2019 · 40.7411, -73.9897Brian Donnelly (KAWS). XX-eyed figures: Mickey Mouse + skull = consumer death. 'Companion' - 45m floating sculpture appeared Hong Kong, Taipei, worldwide. Sotheby's: KAWS 'The KAWS Album' (Simpsons parody) sold $14.8M (2019). Street art → auction house → floating corporate sculpture in Victoria Harbour. The trajectory from graffiti to global capital. Hyperstition: the cartoon that became the commodity that became the monument.
  • Karahan Tepe, Şanlıurfa Province, Turkey archaeological · 2019 · 37.0917, 39.3027Excavated since 2019, this Pre-Pottery Neolithic ritual complex (c. 9400-8200 BCE) is the 'sister site' of Göbekli Tepe, 35 km east, and part of the Taş Tepeler network of at least a dozen sites; its T-shaped stelae and carved figures push the origins of monumental religion back some 11,000 years, before agriculture. Source: Heritage Daily / Ancient Origins, 'Karahan Tepe'.
  • Karnak Temple Obelisks, Luxor, Egypt obelisk · 25.7188, 32.6573Obelisks of Thutmose I and Hatshepsut still stand at Karnak. Egypt's obelisks were carried off by later empires from several temples: the Paris obelisk from nearby Luxor Temple, the London and New York 'Cleopatra's Needles' from Heliopolis via Alexandria. The source of power symbols for every subsequent empire.
  • Kiritimati (Christmas Island), Republic of Kiribati military · 1957-11-08 · 1.8721, -157.4750One of the world's largest atolls by land area (~312 km2). Cook landed on Christmas Eve 1777. Britain's Operation Grapple (1957-58) used it as base; six of its nine nuclear tests were above or near the island (from Grapple X, 8 Nov 1957). The US detonated 24 devices nearby in 1962 (Operation Dominic). Islanders were usually not evacuated.
  • Le Freeport (Singapore Freeport), Changi financial · 2010 · 1.3450, 103.9691Opened 2010 at Changi by Yves Bouvier's group (built for ~S$100M). Art, gold, wine and cars stored duty-suspended; Deutsche Bank kept gold there until 2019. Sold in 2022 to crypto billionaire Jihan Wu's Bitdeer for S$40M.
  • Library of Alexandria, Egypt archaeological · 31.2001, 29.9187One of the largest libraries of the ancient world. It declined gradually over centuries: damage in Caesar's fire (48 BC), the Brucheion quarter destroyed in the 270s and again in 297, the Serapeum daughter library destroyed in 391. The story that it was burned on Caliph Omar's order after the Arab conquest of 642 first appears in Arabic sources ~600 years later and is doubted by historians.
  • London Olympic Park, Stratford - 2012 Summer Olympics surveillance · 2012 · 51.5384, -0.0166£8.77bn against a £9.3bn public funding package. Security relied on extensive CCTV; the G4S security contract failed and troops were called in. East London regeneration displaced working-class communities; legacy housing skewed to luxury flats.
  • Los Angeles Memorial Coliseum - 1984 Summer Olympics governance · 1984 · 34.0141, -118.2879Soviet-led boycott (14 Eastern Bloc nations). Peter Ueberroth's 'private enterprise Olympics' - first to turn a profit ($250M). Created the corporate sponsorship model all future Olympics would follow. The Olympics that proved the Games were a business, not a movement.
  • Louvre Abu Dhabi - Art as Diplomacy museum · 24.5336, 54.3983Under a 30-year intergovernmental deal (2007) Abu Dhabi pays EUR 400M for the Louvre name (to 2037), EUR 190M for art loans, EUR 165M for management advice and more. Designed by Jean Nouvel. Human Rights Watch documented passport confiscation and forced-labour conditions among construction workers. Salvator Mundi's planned showing here was cancelled.
  • Luxembourg Freeport (Luxembourg High Security Hub) - Art Storage financial · 2014 · 49.6398, 6.2220Opened Sept 2014 beside Findel airport, founded by Yves Bouvier; designed by Atelier d'Architecture 3BM3. Same model as Geneva - goods stored with duties suspended. MEPs have criticised it as an enabler of tax evasion. Now the Luxembourg High Security Hub.
  • Luxor Hotel Obelisk, Las Vegas obelisk · 36.0955, -115.1761Las Vegas Luxor: a 30-story glass pyramid with a replica obelisk, a sphinx, and the brightest beam of light on Earth shooting from its apex. Ancient Egyptian sacred architecture replicated as a casino. Pharaonic tomb → gambling hall. The sacred reduced to spectacle. The beam is visible from space. The pyramid that prints money.
  • M+ Museum, West Kowloon, Hong Kong museum · 2021-11-12 · 22.3017, 114.1630Asia's largest museum of visual culture opened in November 2021 under the shadow of Hong Kong's National Security Law; pro-Beijing figures pressured it over its collection and it withheld from display Ai Weiwei's 'Study of Perspective: Tiananmen Square,' which the artist cited as evidence the museum is 'clearly under censorship.' Source: ARTnews; South China Morning Post; Al Jazeera.
  • Machu Picchu, Cusco Region, Peru archaeological · 1911 · -13.1633, -72.5456A 15th-century Inca royal estate perched at ~2,430 m on a ridge above the Urubamba valley, unknown to the outside world until Hiram Bingham publicized it in 1911; its precision ashlar masonry and astronomical alignments (e.g. the Intihuatana stone) survive intact. UNESCO World Heritage since 1983. Source: UNESCO World Heritage 'Historic Sanctuary of Machu Picchu'.
  • Maman (Giant Spider) - Louise Bourgeois, Various Locations obelisk · 1999 · 48.8612, 2.3360Louise Bourgeois, 1999. 30-foot bronze spider. Editions at Guggenheim Bilbao, Tate Modern, National Gallery of Canada, Mori Tower Tokyo, Qatar. Named for the artist's mother ('She was my best friend'). The spider as protector - weaving, repairing, creating. Or: the spider as surveillance, the web as network. Bourgeois: 'Art is a guarantee of sanity.' The mother/monster that guards the museum entrance.
  • Mausoleum of the First Qin Emperor / Terracotta Army, Xi'an, China archaeological · 1974 · 34.3817, 109.2539The tomb complex of Qin Shi Huang (d. 210 BC), guarded by an estimated 8,000 life-size terracotta soldiers discovered by well-diggers in 1974; the central burial mound, described by historian Sima Qian as containing rivers of mercury, remains unexcavated. UNESCO World Heritage since 1987. Source: UNESCO World Heritage 'Mausoleum of the First Qin Emperor'.
  • Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York - Board Patterns museum · 2021 · 40.7794, -73.9632Trustees and donors include/included David Koch ($65M plaza), Henry Kravis and Leonard Lauder (Cubist collection gift). The Sackler Wing (Temple of Dendur) bore the name of the family whose Purdue Pharma made OxyContin, a driver of the US opioid epidemic; the name was removed in 2021 after protests.
  • Mexico City Olympic Sites - 1968 Summer Olympics conflict · 1968-10-02 · 19.4515, -99.1365Tlatelolco massacre, 2 Oct 1968 - ten days before the opening ceremony. Mexican army and the Olympia Battalion, a secret government security unit, fired on student protesters in the Plaza de las Tres Culturas: 44 deaths documented by name, with estimates of 300-400. The Games went ahead. Tommie Smith and John Carlos raised fists on the podium and were suspended and expelled from the Games.
  • Mohenjo-daro, Larkana District, Sindh, Pakistan archaeological · 1980 · 27.3253, 68.1349One of the largest cities of the Indus Valley Civilization (built c. 2500 BC), notable for grid-planned streets, a covered drainage system and the 'Great Bath'; its still-undeciphered script leaves a sophisticated urban society largely unreadable. UNESCO listed it in 1980 and warns of severe erosion. Source: UNESCO World Heritage 'Archaeological Ruins at Moenjodaro'.
  • Monte Verde, Chile archaeological · -41.5047, -73.2044Pre-Clovis site near Puerto Montt. Monte Verde II, dated ~14,500 years ago and largely accepted, showed people were in South America at least ~1,000 years before Clovis and overturned the 'Clovis first' model after years of resistance. An older layer (MV-I, ~18,500 cal BP) remains contested.
  • Montreal Olympic Stadium - 1976 Summer Olympics financial · 1976 · 45.5579, -73.5516$1.5B cost - 'The Big Owe.' Took 30 years to pay off (2006). Mayor Jean Drapeau: 'The Olympics can no more have a deficit than a man can have a baby.' Retractable roof never worked properly. The stadium whose debt outlasted a generation.
  • Munich Olympic Village - 1972 Summer Olympics conflict · 1972 · 48.1755, 11.5518Munich Massacre: 11 Israeli athletes killed by Black September. German police botched rescue at Fürstenfeldbruck airfield. Mossad launched Operation Wrath of God - targeted assassinations across Europe. The Olympics that became a war zone. Games continued after 34-hour pause. 'The Games must go on.' - Avery Brundage.
  • Museo Egizio, Turin museum · 1824 · 45.0684, 7.6844Founded in 1824, the oldest museum devoted solely to ancient Egypt, with more than 40,000 artifacts - considered the most important Egyptological collection after Cairo - much of it amassed by French consul Bernardino Drovetti during the colonial-era scramble for Egyptian antiquities. Source: Museo Egizio; Encyclopaedia Britannica.
  • Museo del Prado, Madrid museum · 1819-11-19 · 40.4138, -3.6921Opened 1819 from the Spanish royal collection: Velázquez, Goya, El Greco, Bosch. The Habsburg and Bourbon crowns that assembled it drew silver from Potosí, worked by forced indigenous (mita) and enslaved labour, and ruled one of the largest empires in history. Las Meninas was painted while Potosí's silver was arriving in Seville.
  • Museum of Islamic Art, Doha, Qatar museum · 2011 · 25.2959, 51.5390Designed by I.M. Pei. Qatar Museums (Sheikha Al-Mayassa bint Hamad Al Thani): estimated $1B/year art spending. Qatar bought Cézanne's 'The Card Players' for $250M+ (2011) - highest price ever at the time. The nation-state art collection as soft power infrastructure. Gas wealth converted to cultural capital.
  • Museum of the Bible, Washington D.C. museum · 2017 · 38.8845, -77.0165Funded by Hobby Lobby's Green family. In 2017 Hobby Lobby paid a $3M fine and agreed to forfeit more than 5,500 smuggled Iraqi artifacts; the museum later agreed to return over 11,000 objects to Egypt and Iraq, and the looted Gilgamesh Dream Tablet was repatriated to Iraq in 2021. Source: U.S. DOJ; Smithsonian Magazine.
  • Musée du Louvre, Paris museum · 48.8606, 2.3376615,000+ objects, 35,000 on display. Originally a royal palace. Under Napoleon it became the Musée Napoléon, filled with art seized from conquered states; Vivant Denon, who accompanied Napoleon to Egypt, directed it. The Mona Lisa was brought to France by Leonardo and acquired by Francis I after his death in 1519. The museum as empire.
  • Musée du quai Branly – Jacques Chirac, Paris museum · 2018 · 48.8610, 2.2980The museum holds around 70,000 sub-Saharan African objects — about two-thirds of France's African holdings; the 2018 Sarr-Savoy report, which estimated 90-95% of Africa's heritage sits outside the continent, prompted France to return 26 works plundered from Abomey Palace in 1892 to Benin. Source: Center for Art Law; Cultural Property News; Artnet.
  • Nalanda University, Bihar, India archaeological · 1200 · 25.1357, 85.4428Buddhist monastic university founded in the 5th century CE; likely attacked and ransacked by Bakhtiyar Khalji's forces c. 1200 CE. Its library's size is unknown - estimated in the hundreds of thousands of volumes; the popular 'nine million manuscripts' has no documentary source.
  • National Museum of Afghanistan, Kabul museum · 1992 · 34.4649, 69.1200During the 1990s civil war and Taliban rule, an estimated 70% of the museum's roughly 100,000-object collection was looted or destroyed, including some 2,500 statues smashed as idolatrous in 2001; the fabled Bactrian Gold survived, hidden in Central Bank vaults and rediscovered in 2003. Source: Britannica; Artnet News; Science (AAAS).
  • National Museum of Anthropology, Mexico City museum · 1964 · 19.4260, -99.1861Aztec Sun Stone, Olmec colossal heads, Maya jade masks; 600,000+ artefacts. Built 1964 by the modern Mexican state to present a pre-Hispanic heritage destroyed by the Spanish conquest. On 25 Dec 1985 two students stole 124 artefacts; most were recovered in 1989. The museum as the state's claim to a heritage it inherited from conquest.
  • National Museum of Brazil, Rio de Janeiro museum · 2018-09-02 · -22.9055, -43.2253Brazil's oldest scientific institution (1818), in the former Imperial Palace; ~20 million items. Fire on 2 Sept 2018 destroyed most of the collection (reported 92.5%), after years of budget cuts (maintenance reportedly ~$13,000/year - attributed). Luzia, an 11,500-year-old skeleton, was fragmented in the fire; most of her remains were recovered.
  • National Museum of China, Beijing museum · 2003 · 39.9042, 116.3975East side of Tiananmen Square. 1.3 million objects. Formed 2003 from the Museum of the Revolution and the Museum of Chinese History. Its permanent exhibitions frame 5,000 years of history as leading to Communist Party rule, on the square where the 1989 protests were crushed.
  • National Palace Museum, Taipei museum · 1948 · 25.1024, 121.5485696,000+ objects — Chinese imperial collection spanning 8,000 years. Chiang Kai-shek evacuated the collection from Beijing's Forbidden City (1948-49) during the Chinese Civil War — 2,972 crates shipped to Taiwan in three shipments. The mainland government calls it theft. Taiwan calls it preservation. The museum whose entire collection is a political argument about which China is the real one.
  • Natural History Museum, London museum · 1881 · 51.4961, -0.176480 million specimens. Founded 1881 from British Museum's natural history collection. Darwin's specimens. Colonial-era botanical, zoological, and geological specimens collected from every continent Britain controlled. Specimen collecting was mapping for extraction — catalogue the resources, then send the companies. The museum as inventory ledger for the empire's resource base.
  • Nazca Lines, Nazca, Ica, Peru archaeological · 1994 · -14.6998, -75.1853Hundreds of giant geoglyphs - animals, plants and straight lines up to kilometers long - etched into the desert plateau by the Nazca culture between roughly 500 BC and AD 500, only fully legible from the air; ongoing drone surveys keep adding newly discovered figures. UNESCO World Heritage since 1994. Source: UNESCO World Heritage 'Lines and Geoglyphs of Nasca and Palpa'.
  • Neue Galerie New York museum · 2006 · 40.7813, -73.9603The museum's centerpiece is Gustav Klimt's 'Portrait of Adele Bloch-Bauer I' (the 'Woman in Gold'), Nazi-looted from a Jewish Viennese family and restituted to heir Maria Altmann in 2006 after a U.S. Supreme Court case, then bought by museum co-founder Ronald Lauder for a reported $135 million — a landmark in Holocaust art-restitution. Source: The New York Times; Republic of Austria v. Altmann (2004).
  • Pergamon Museum, Berlin museum · 52.5212, 13.3967Ishtar Gate of Babylon, Pergamon Altar, Market Gate of Miletus - whole ancient structures excavated abroad and rebuilt in Berlin. Closed since Oct 2023 for renovation, expected mostly closed until 2037-2043.
  • Persepolis (Takht-e Jamshid), Fars Province, Iran archaeological · 1979 · 29.9352, 52.8904Ceremonial capital of the Achaemenid Persian Empire, begun c. 518 BC by Darius I, with its Apadana audience hall and reliefs of tribute-bearing nations; it was looted and burned by Alexander the Great's army in 330 BC. A UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1979. Source: UNESCO World Heritage 'Persepolis' / Britannica.
  • Pine Ridge Reservation, South Dakota governance · 43.1000, -102.5500Oglala Lakota reservation. The North American pole of inaccessibility (the point farthest from any coast) lies within it, ~11 km north of Allen. Separately, the Black Hills (He Sapa), outside the reservation, were taken after the gold rush in breach of the 1868 treaty; Mount Rushmore was carved on the Lakota Six Grandfathers.
  • Puma Punku, Tiwanaku, Bolivia archaeological · -16.5617, -68.6805Terraced platform mound of the Tiwanaku culture, built c. AD 536-600, faced with finely cut andesite and sandstone blocks - including the interlocking 'H-blocks' - joined with cast copper-arsenic-nickel cramps. ~3,850 m (12,600 ft) altitude. Claims of machine-precision tolerances and anachronistic technology come from ancient-astronaut literature and have no archaeological support.
  • PyeongChang Olympic Complex - 2018 Winter Olympics governance · 2018 · 37.6319, 128.6786Reported cost ~US$13bn. Held months after peak nuclear tension with the DPRK. Kim Yo-jong attended the opening; the two Koreas marched under the Korean Unification Flag and fielded a unified women's hockey team. The Olympics as diplomatic theatre.
  • Rani ki Vav stepwell, Patan, Gujarat, India archaeological · 23.8587, 72.101711th-century stepwell attributed to Queen Udayamati, descending seven levels to the water with more than 500 principal sculptures. Silted over, rediscovered in the 1940s; UNESCO World Heritage site.
  • Rijksmuseum, Amsterdam museum · 52.3600, 4.8852Dutch Golden Age collection. Rembrandt's Night Watch. Vermeer's Milkmaid. The 'Golden Age' was funded by the VOC (Dutch East India Company) — the world's first multinational corporation, first to issue stock, and the organization that colonized Indonesia, South Africa, and controlled the global spice trade through military force. The museum celebrates the art produced by the profits of the first corporate empire.
  • Rio Olympic Park, Barra da Tijuca - 2016 Summer Olympics financial · 2016 · -22.9714, -43.3953Reported total cost ~US$13bn (sports-related costs ~US$4.6bn per the Oxford study). Favela clearances; sewage in Guanabara Bay; the state of Rio declared a financial emergency weeks before opening. In April 2017 Brazil's Supreme Court opened an investigation of former mayor Eduardo Paes on Odebrecht plea testimony alleging ~US$4.8m solicited in 2012 for Olympic contracts; he denies it and no outcome is recorded here.
  • Royal Museum for Central Africa, Tervuren, Belgium museum · 1897 · 50.8312, 4.5224Built to showcase Leopold II's Congo Free State at the 1897 International Exposition, financed by profits from a forced-labour rubber regime under which millions died (estimates range widely, up to ~10 million - contested). For a century it presented the colonial 'civilising mission'. Reopened 2018 as the AfricaMuseum; the building itself is the artefact.
  • Salt Lake City - 2002 Winter Olympics financial · 2002 · 40.7608, -111.8910Bribery scandal (broke Nov 1998): IOC members received cash, scholarships for children, medical care and land deals from the bid committee. Ten IOC members were expelled and ten sanctioned - the IOC's first sanctions for corruption. Bid leaders Tom Welch and Dave Johnson were charged with bribery and fraud and acquitted of all charges in Dec 2003.
  • Salvator Mundi Sale, Christie's NYC - $450.3M financial · 2017 · 40.7587, -73.9787Leonardo da Vinci 'Salvator Mundi' - $450.3M (15 Nov 2017), record for any painting at auction. Bought by Prince Badr bin Abdullah, reported to be a stand-in for Mohammed bin Salman (attributed). Bought in 2005 for $1,175 as 'after Leonardo'. Attribution disputed by scholars. Not publicly exhibited since the sale; reported to be in storage in Saudi Arabia - location attributed, not documented. A planned Louvre Abu Dhabi showing was cancelled without explanation.
  • Sanxingdui Ruins, Guanghan, Sichuan, China archaeological · 1986 · 30.9937, 104.1999Sacrificial pits at this Bronze Age site (c. 1700-1150 BC), first probed in 1929 and dramatically re-excavated from 2019, yielded hundreds of bronze masks, heads and trees - including a mask 1.31 m wide - from a lost Shu civilization with no written records, whose art style is unmatched anywhere else in ancient China. Source: World Archaeology, 'The lost world of Sanxingdui' / China Daily.
  • Sarajevo Olympic Venues - 1984 Winter Olympics conflict · 1984 · 43.8563, 18.4131Beautiful venues built 1984. By 1992: bobsled track used as artillery position. Zetra Olympic Hall: burned, used as morgue. Athletes' Village: sniper positions. The Olympic venues that became a battlefield within 8 years. Siege of Sarajevo: 1,425 days, 11,541 killed. The fastest transformation from celebration to slaughter.
  • Smithsonian Institution, Washington D.C. museum · 38.8881, -77.0259Holds over 157 million items across 21 museums. Online claims that it suppresses 'giant skeleton' finds from 19th-century Bureau of Ethnology reports have no documentary support - unsupported.
  • Sochi Olympic Park, Russia - 2014 Winter Olympics conflict · 2014 · 43.4028, 39.9556$51B - most expensive Olympics in history. Built on coast of historical Circassia. Circassian Genocide (1864): Russian Empire killed/expelled 1-1.5M Circassians. Russia hosted its celebration games on the land of a genocide it has never acknowledged. Sochi was the port from which Circassians were expelled. The victory lap on a mass grave.
  • Sotheby's, New Bond Street, London - Major Auction House financial · 1744 · 51.5132, -0.1425Founded 1744. Acquired by Patrick Drahi in 2019 (~$3.7bn). Dmitry Rybolovlev accused Swiss dealer Yves Bouvier of overcharging him by nearly $1bn on art bought partly via Sotheby's; the cases against Bouvier were dismissed and the two settled in Dec 2023, and a New York jury cleared Sotheby's on all counts in Jan 2024. The affair exposed how private-sale markups work.
  • St. Helena, South Atlantic military · 1815 · -15.9650, -5.7089Napoleon exiled here (1815-1821). Only accessible by ship until airport opened 2017. British East India Company administered until 1834. Strategic mid-Atlantic position. The island designed to imprison an emperor - so remote it didn't need walls.
  • Tate Modern, London - Turbine Hall museum · 2000 · 51.5076, -0.0994Unilever Series funded Turbine Hall commissions (2000-2012). BP sponsorship of Tate: protested relentlessly by Liberate Tate. BP dropped 2016 after 26 years. Tate board included oil executives while exhibiting climate-themed art. The oil company sponsoring the museum that showed art about environmental destruction.
  • The Broad, Los Angeles museum · 34.0544, -118.2508Eli Broad (SunAmerica, KB Home; d. 2021) and Edythe Broad financed the ~$140M building on Grand Avenue to house their own collection (Basquiat, Koons, Warhol, Hirst). Broad also gave $30M to rescue MOCA (2008) across the street and funded LACMA's BCAM. Art philanthropy as immortality project.
  • The Mob Museum, Las Vegas museum · 2012 · 36.1728, -115.1414Officially the National Museum of Organized Crime and Law Enforcement, it opened in 2012 inside the former federal courthouse that hosted a 1950-51 Kefauver Committee hearing on organized crime, documenting the mob's role in building Las Vegas and its casino skim operations. Source: The Mob Museum (themobmuseum.org); Las Vegas Review-Journal.
  • Tokyo Olympic Stadium - 2020/2021 Summer Olympics financial · 2021 · 35.6778, 139.7134Postponed by COVID - the only postponement in Olympic history - and held in 2021 in empty stadiums; reported cost ~US$15bn. Zaha Hadid's stadium design was scrapped over cost. Organising-committee executive board member Haruyuki Takahashi was arrested for bribery in 2022; Dentsu was the Games' exclusive marketing agency.
  • Topkapi Palace Museum, Istanbul museum · 1924 · 41.0115, 28.9834Ottoman imperial residence (1478-1853). Holds relics attributed to Muhammad (sword, cloak) and claimed relics of Moses and Joseph. The Harem: some 300-400 rooms. After the sultanate was abolished (1922), the palace became a museum in 1924. The seat of an empire spanning Europe and Asia, now a tourist site.
  • Tulsa Convention Hall - 1921 Detention Camp military · 1921 · 36.1558, -95.9919Convention Hall (now the Tulsa Theater), McNulty Park and the fairgrounds were used to intern up to 6,000 Black residents of Greenwood during the 1921 massacre. Under martial law detainees needed identification cards and release required a white person to vouch for them; meanwhile homes were looted and burned. Guardsmen fired on Black neighbourhoods, including with a machine gun (attributed).
  • Tulsa Mass Graves - Oaklawn Cemetery conflict · 1921 · 36.1485, -95.9834Oaklawn Cemetery, Tulsa. Eyewitness accounts describe victims of the 1921 massacre buried in unmarked graves, dumped in the river or burned (attributed). The official death toll was 36 (26 Black, 10 white); estimates run to ~300. In October 2020 a forensic team unearthed 11 coffins in a suspected mass grave; later excavations recovered remains with gunshot wounds. Identification continues more than a century later.
  • Uffizi Gallery, Florence museum · 1581 · 43.7678, 11.2553Gallery established 1581 in the Medici offices built by Vasari. The Medici - bankers to the papacy, later dukes, and the source of several popes - used art patronage as a display of power. The gallery as ledger.
  • Valley of the Kings, Luxor, Egypt archaeological · 1922 · 25.7402, 32.6014Royal necropolis with 65 known tombs and chambers, used c. 1539-1075 BC. Most were looted in antiquity; Tutankhamun's tomb (KV62) was found intact in 1922. Radar surveys from 2015 for hidden chambers behind KV62 produced conflicting results.
  • Vatican Secret Archives (Apostolic Archive), Vatican City museum · 2019 · 41.9022, 12.453985 linear kilometers of shelving. Documents spanning 12+ centuries. 'Secret' renamed 'Private' (2019). Access restricted to qualified scholars by application. Contains records of Inquisition, Galileo trial, excommunications, papal bulls authorizing colonization (Doctrine of Discovery). What the church chooses to preserve and who it allows to see it.
  • Victoria and Albert Museum, London museum · 1868 · 51.4969, -0.1716The V&A holds treasures looted by British forces after the 1868 Battle of Maqdala in Ethiopia — gold crowns, crosses and royal regalia; in 2018 director Tristram Hunt publicly offered to return the Maqdala collection to Ethiopia on long-term loan rather than as outright restitution, spotlighting UK museums' colonial acquisitions. Source: Victoria and Albert Museum (vam.ac.uk); The Guardian.
  • Visočica Hill (Bosnian Pyramid), Bosnia archaeological · 43.9767, 18.1764Natural hill promoted since 2005 by Semir Osmanagić as a 'Bosnian pyramid'. Direct study by geologists and archaeologists found the hills are natural flatiron formations with no sign of construction; the European Association of Archaeologists called the claim 'a cruel hoax'. Recorded as a killed specimen.
  • Çatalhöyük, Çumra, Konya Province, Turkey archaeological · 2012 · 37.6667, 32.8281A 9,000-year-old Neolithic proto-city of densely packed mudbrick houses entered through the roof, housing up to ~8,000 people with no streets, elaborate wall paintings and burials beneath the floors - a key site for understanding the origins of settled urban life. UNESCO World Heritage since 2012. Source: UNESCO World Heritage 'Neolithic Site of Çatalhöyük'.

Section XIV - 56 locations

  • Arctic - Drilling Frontier mining · 71.0000, 25.0000Arctic oil and gas development by Russia (Gazprom, Rosneft) and Norway (Equinor) in the Barents region expands as sea ice retreats.
  • Bayan Obo, Inner Mongolia, China - Rare Earths mining · 41.7808, 109.9697World's largest known rare-earth deposit. China mined about 69% of the world's rare earths in 2025 (USGS: 270,000 of 390,000 t). Rare earths go into fighter jets, guided missiles, satellites, smartphones and MRI machines - the material basis for Section X's surveillance technology and for military hardware.
  • Berkeley Pit, Butte, Montana mining · 2016-11-28 · 46.0172, -112.5117Former open-pit copper mine (1955-1982; Anaconda, then ARCO), part of a Superfund site listed in 1983. About 1.6 km long and 0.8 km wide, filled with roughly 270 m (900 ft) of acidic, metal-laden water. Snow geese die on it: 342 carcasses were recovered in 1996, and on 28 November 2016 tens of thousands landed on the pit.
  • Bingham Canyon Mine, Utah - Kennecott/Rio Tinto mining · 2013-04 · 40.5233, -112.1497The largest human-made excavation and deepest open-pit mine in the world: over 1.2 km deep and 4 km wide, mined since 1906, now by Rio Tinto's Kennecott subsidiary. It has produced more copper than any mine in history - over 17 million tonnes. In April 2013 a slide inside the pit, possibly the largest non-volcanic landslide in North American history, buried part of the pit. Mining continued.
  • Broken Hill, Australia - Origin of BHP mining · 1885 · -31.9505, 141.4683BHP - the Broken Hill Proprietary Company - was founded here in 1885 by Charles Rasp and six partners to mine silver, lead and zinc. Now BHP Group, the world's largest mining company by market capitalisation (2025), operating worldwide. The company still carries the name of its first mine.
  • Carajás Mine, Pará, Brazil - Iron Ore mining · 2019 · -6.0800, -50.1500Vale's Carajás complex, the largest iron ore mine in the world. Same company: Vale's Brumadinho tailings dam in Minas Gerais collapsed on 25 Jan 2019, killing 272 people; Vale managers and TÜV SÜD engineers who had certified the dam were arrested, and prosecutors allege the risk was known (allegation, not a finding).
  • Cerrejón, Colombia - Coal Mine mining · 11.0833, -72.6667Largest coal mine in Latin America (over 690 km2), now owned by Glencore (formerly shared with BHP and Anglo American). In June 2020 lawyers for local Wayuu communities asked the UN special rapporteur to halt work over environmental harm; stream diversions for expansion are contested.
  • Chuquicamata, Chile - World's Largest Copper Open-Pit mining · 1973-09-11 · -22.3214, -68.9014Codelco's open pit, among the largest by excavated volume; mined industrially since 1915 under the Guggenheims and then Anaconda. Allende's government nationalised copper in 1971 ('copper is Chile's wage'), taking Anaconda's and Kennecott's mines; ITT had offered the CIA $1 million in 1970 to stop Allende (attributed). The CIA funded his opponents; its role in the 11 September 1973 coup itself is contested. Nationalisation and coup share a timeline - that is not a chain.
  • Churchill, Manitoba - Northern Port mining · 2018 · 58.7684, -94.1650Hudson Bay deep-water port (four Panamax-capable berths) linked south only by the Hudson Bay Railway; open roughly late July to early November. The federal government sold it to US firm OmniTRAX in 1997; OmniTRAX shut it in 2016 and sold port and railway in 2018 to Arctic Gateway Group, a First Nations and community consortium. Grain and Arctic resupply are its trade; ships reach it through Hudson Strait, not the Northwest Passage.
  • Eastern Congo / DRC - Cobalt Mines conflict · -3.4500, 28.0000Children as young as 6 in artisanal cobalt mining. Cobalt → batteries → surveillance cameras → smart cities. The supply chain is built on child labor.
  • El Teniente Copper Mine, Chile mining · 2025-07-31 · -34.0878, -70.3875The world's largest underground copper mine, with more than 3,000 km of tunnels, run by state-owned Codelco in the Andes east of Rancagua. Industrial mining began in 1906 under the US Braden Copper Company (later Kennecott) before Chile nationalised it in 1971. A collapse after a tremor on 31 July 2025 killed six miners.
  • Escondida Mine, Chile - Copper mining · -24.2667, -69.0667World's largest copper mine (about 1.28 million tonnes of copper in 2024, roughly 5% of world mine output). BHP 57.5%, Rio Tinto 30%, Japanese partners 12.5%. Copper for wiring, circuit boards, data centres and submarine cables.
  • Foxconn - Zhengzhou iPhone plant / Longhua, Shenzhen corporate · 2010 · 34.5535, 113.8415Foxconn's Zhengzhou Technology Park assembles the bulk of Apple's iPhones (about 200,000 workers in Nov 2022; COVID lockdown unrest there that autumn). The 2010 suicide cluster was at its Longhua campus in Shenzhen, 'Foxconn City', where the company installed safety nets; a Zhengzhou worker's suicide was reported in 2016.
  • Ghawar Field, Saudi Arabia - World's Largest Oil mining · 2019 · 25.4000, 49.5000By far the largest conventional oil field in the world (about 280 x 30 km), roughly a third of Saudi Arabia's cumulative oil output. Operated by Saudi Aramco, listed on 11 Dec 2019 at about $1.9 trillion and above $2 trillion the next day. Saudi Arabia's Public Investment Fund, an Aramco shareholder, put a reported $2 billion into Jared Kushner's Affinity Partners.
  • Grasberg Mine, Papua, Indonesia mining · -4.0620, 137.1112Copper-gold mine run by PT Freeport Indonesia (Indonesian state 51.23%, Freeport-McMoRan 48.77% since 2018), on Amungme and Kamoro land. Between 1998 and 2004 Freeport paid Indonesian military and police nearly $20 million (NYT, 2005). Norway's pension fund excluded Freeport and Rio Tinto over its environmental damage. Henry Kissinger sat on Freeport's board (attributed).
  • Greenbushes Lithium Mine, Western Australia mining · -33.8684, 116.0662World's largest hard-rock lithium mine by reserves, output and capacity: about 1.95 million tonnes of spodumene concentrate a year (2020), enough for a third of world demand. Run by Talison Lithium, a joint venture of China's Tianqi Lithium (51%) and Albemarle (49%), 257 km south of Perth.
  • Groningen Gas Field, Netherlands mining · 2024 · 53.3500, 6.8500Largest natural-gas field in Europe, producing from 1963. Extraction caused subsidence and, from 1991, induced earthquakes (largest: M3.6 at Huizinge, 2012) that damaged houses across the province; the National Ombudsman called it a 'national crisis' (2021). The field was closed in 2024.
  • Jwaneng Diamond Mine, Botswana mining · -24.5845, 24.7298Nicknamed the 'Prince of Mines,' Jwaneng is the world's richest diamond mine by value, producing 12-15 million carats a year and generating 60-70% of Debswana's revenue. It is run by Debswana, a 50-50 joint venture between the Government of Botswana and the De Beers Group, and is moving underground to extend its life by 20 years. Source: Debswana / Mining Technology (debswana.com/jwaneng).
  • Kalgoorlie Super Pit (Fimiston Open Pit), Australia mining · 1893 · -30.7747, 121.5094One of Australia's largest open-pit gold mines, about 3.5 km long, 1.6 km wide and over 675 m deep on the historic Golden Mile, producing about 430,000-460,000 oz of gold a year. Owned by Northern Star Resources since 2020; it consolidated many 1890s underground leases into one pit.
  • Kimberley, South Africa - De Beers 'Big Hole' mining · 1888 · -28.7282, 24.7499Cecil Rhodes founded De Beers in 1888. The Big Hole was long considered the largest hand-dug excavation on Earth (a 2005 re-examination suggests Jagersfontein or Bultfontein may be larger). Diamonds -> De Beers monopoly -> 'A Diamond Is Forever' (1947) -> managed scarcity. Rhodes' fortune funds the Rhodes Scholarships (Bill Clinton, Pete Buttigieg, Susan Rice, Rachel Maddow) and financed the Round Table movement, which is credited with influencing the Council on Foreign Relations (attributed; Section VII).
  • Kipushi, DRC - Zinc/Copper Mine mining · 1924 · -11.7603, 27.2453Underground zinc-copper mine (formerly Prince Léopold Mine), producing from the 1920s to 1993 under Belgian colonial and then Gécamines operation. Now Ivanhoe Mines 68%, Gécamines 32%.
  • Kolwezi, DRC - Cobalt Mining mining · -10.7167, 25.4667Heart of the DRC cobalt belt (Lualaba). Glencore operates Kamoto Copper Company (KCC: Glencore 70%, Gécamines 25%, DRC state 5%, per KCC) and Mutanda (Glencore 95%), about 40 km east. The DRC mined about 73% of the world's cobalt in 2025 (USGS). Amnesty (2016) found children as young as seven in artisanal mining. The US Labor Department lists DRC cobalt for child labour (since 2009) and for forced labour of adults (2024), and lists Chinese lithium-ion batteries made with it (2024).
  • Lubumbashi, DRC - Copper/Cobalt Hub mining · -11.6647, 27.4794Capital of Haut-Katanga and commercial hub of the copper-cobalt belt; seat of state miner Gécamines. Chinese firms, among them CMOC (Tenke Fungurume, in neighbouring Lualaba), are leading operators. The US Labor Department (2024) lists DRC cobalt for child labour and for forced labour of adults, 'prevalent ... in the Copperbelt region, particularly in Haut-Katanga and Lualaba.'
  • Magadan, Russia - Gateway to the Gulag blacksite · 1996 · 59.5680, 150.8083Port and base of Dalstroy (1931), which ran some 80 Gulag camps in Kolyma mining gold and other metals; its prisoner count reached about 200,000 (1952). The R504 Kolyma Highway (2,031 km), built by prisoners, is called the 'Road of Bones'; that the dead were buried in the roadbed is a popular account not confirmed by remains. 10,251 deaths were recorded in the Kolyma camps in 1938 alone; totals are contested. Mask of Sorrow by Ernst Neizvestny, unveiled 12 June 1996.
  • Marikana, South Africa - Lonmin Platinum Massacre mining · 2012-08-16 · -25.6910, 27.489316 August 2012: South African Police Service shot dead 34 striking Lonmin rock-drill operators and wounded 78; ten others, including police and guards, had died in the days before. The strikers wanted R12,500 a month. Cyril Ramaphosa, then a Lonmin board member, emailed that the events were 'dastardly criminal' and needed 'concomitant action'; he apologised for the phrasing in 2017. The Farlam Commission absolved him of wrongdoing and found police commanders had tried to mislead the public and the inquiry. Lonmin was acquired by Sibanye-Stillwater (2019).
  • Mir Mine (Mirny Diamond Pipe), Russia mining · 1957 · 62.5285, 113.9925One of the world's largest excavated diamond pipes, an open pit about 1,200 m wide and 525 m deep in Yakutia. Discovered 1955 and opened 1957; the open-pit stage ended in 2001 and Alrosa moved underground. Flooding in 2017 trapped over 140 miners; eight died.
  • Monsanto HQ (now Bayer), Creve Coeur, Missouri corporate · 2018-06-07 · 38.6600, -90.4227Monsanto made PCBs, DDT, Agent Orange and Roundup (glyphosate). Bayer completed its US$66bn takeover on 7 June 2018 and retired the name. Bayer was one of the companies merged into IG Farben (1925), which used concentration-camp slave labour and co-owned Degesch, maker of Zyklon B (attributed). Seed patents bar replanting (Bowman v. Monsanto, 2013). The food supply as intellectual property.
  • Morenci Mine, Arizona - Freeport-McMoRan mining · 1903 · 33.0836, -109.3331One of the largest copper mines in North America, now Freeport-McMoRan's (which absorbed Phelps Dodge in 2007). The 1903 Morenci strike by mostly Mexican-American miners ended when a flash flood killed 40-50 people before an expected clash with troops. In the 1917 Bisbee Deportation, Phelps Dodge and sheriff's deputies loaded about 1,300 striking miners onto cattle cars and left them in the New Mexico desert.
  • Mount Weld, Western Australia - Rare Earths mining · -28.8600, 122.5478Lynas Rare Earths' mine near Laverton. Its concentrate feeds Lynas's plant in Malaysia, the largest rare-earth production facility outside China. Australia's main bid to break China's hold on rare earths for defence and technology.
  • Mountain Pass Mine, California - U.S. Rare Earths mining · 35.4775, -115.5347The only rare-earth mining and processing site in the United States (15.8% of world output in 2020), owned since 2017 by MP Materials, whose largest holders were JHL Capital, QVT Financial and CEO James Litinsky, with China's Shenghe Resources holding about 7.7%. In July 2025 the Department of Defense agreed a deal making it MP's largest shareholder. China mined about 69% of the world's rare earths in 2025 (USGS) and dominates processing.
  • Muruntau Gold Mine, Uzbekistan mining · 1969 · 41.4967, 64.5778One of the world's largest open-pit gold mines - about 3.5 km long, 2.7 km wide and 600 m deep - second by output after Grasberg (61 t in 2014). Run by Uzbekistan's state Navoi Mining & Metallurgical Combinat; industrial mining since 21 July 1969; reserves estimated at 71.4 million ounces.
  • Nauru mining · 1906 · -0.5228, 166.9315Smallest republic on Earth. Phosphate mining stripped 80% of the island (1906-2002). Richest per-capita country in 1970s, now bankrupt. Australian offshore immigration detention center. Mined to dust, then used as a prison island. The lifecycle of extraction: use it, empty it, fill it with people no one wants.
  • Nestlé HQ, Vevey, Switzerland corporate · 1977-07-04 · 46.4603, 6.8413World's largest food company. Its infant-formula marketing in poor countries, where formula was often mixed with unsafe water, led to a boycott launched in the US on 4 July 1977. Water-bottling disputes in Michigan, California and Pakistan. Chairman Peter Brabeck-Letmathe said in 2005 (We Feed the World) that declaring water a public right was 'an extreme solution' and that water should have a market value; he later said drinking water is a human right.
  • Niger Delta, Nigeria - Oil Extraction mining · 1995-11-10 · 4.8156, 6.4457Shell, ExxonMobil and Chevron have pumped oil here since the 1950s amid repeated spills. Ken Saro-Wiwa, writer and leader of the Ogoni campaign against Shell's pollution, was hanged with eight others on 10 November 1995 after a special military tribunal convicted them of murders they denied; the trial was condemned internationally. The writer killed for documenting the extraction.
  • Norilsk, Krasnoyarsk Krai, Russia mining · 1935 · 69.3535, 88.2027Arctic mining city built by Gulag labour: Norillag held 1,200 prisoners in 1935 and 72,500 at its 1951 peak; Memorial estimates about 400,000 passed through. Nornickel is a leading producer of palladium and nickel. A closed city, re-closed to foreigners in 2001. No road link to the rest of Russia; freight rail runs only to the Yenisei port of Dudinka. Repeatedly listed among the world's most polluted places (attributed).
  • Ok Tedi Mine, Papua New Guinea - BHP Environmental Disaster mining · 1999 · -5.2114, 141.1394Ok Tedi copper-gold mine, operated by BHP until 2002. In 1999 BHP reported that about 90 million tonnes of mine waste a year had been discharged into the Ok Tedi and Fly rivers for over a decade, destroying downstream villages, farms and fisheries; about 1,588 km2 of forest has died or is under stress. BHP's CEO said the mine was 'not compatible with our environmental values'. BHP left in 2002 by transferring its stake to the PNG Sustainable Development Program.
  • Olympic Dam, South Australia - BHP Uranium mining · 2012 · -30.4500, 136.8833BHP's underground copper-uranium-gold-silver mine (since 1988): the world's largest known single uranium deposit. A planned open-pit expansion was postponed indefinitely in August 2012. The Roxby Downs (Indenture Ratification) Act 1982 set the mine's legal framework; Aboriginal elders, including Arabana elder Kevin Buzzacott, have challenged its approvals.
  • Oyu Tolgoi, Mongolia - Copper/Gold mining · 43.0000, 106.8500Copper-gold mine in the Gobi: Rio Tinto (via Turquoise Hill) 66%, Government of Mongolia 34%. Development cost rose from US$4.6bn (2010) to about $10bn (2013). Herders say it drains the region's water - it uses over a billion gallons a month. Rio Tinto also destroyed the Juukan Gorge rock shelters in Western Australia, with 46,000 years of human occupation, in May 2020.
  • Panguna Mine, Bougainville, PNG - Rio Tinto Civil War mining · 1988 · -6.3000, 155.4833Open-pit copper-gold mine run 1972-1989 by Bougainville Copper Ltd, a Rio Tinto (CRA) subsidiary. Landowner anger over pollution and revenue fed the Bougainville Civil War (1988-1998); estimates of Bougainvillean dead run from 15,000 to 20,000. After the rebels declared independence in May 1990, PNG blockaded the island with UH-1 helicopters and patrol boats Australia had supplied as aid. Closed since 1989.
  • Perm-36, Ural Region, Russia blacksite · 1987-12 · 58.2631, 57.4321Soviet forced-labour colony ITK-6 near Kuchino, built 1946; from 1972 a strict- and special-regime camp for 'especially dangerous state criminals', mostly dissidents. Closed December 1987. Preserved by Memorial as the only surviving Gulag camp and opened in 1995 as the Museum of the History of Political Repression; regional authorities withdrew support and the NGO museum closed in April 2014. Its state-run successor was reported to recast the camp's history (attributed).
  • Permian Basin, Texas/New Mexico - Oil & Gas mining · 31.9500, -102.1700Highest-producing oil field in the US (about 4.2 million barrels a day in 2019), across west Texas and southeast New Mexico. Major operators include ExxonMobil, Chevron and ConocoPhillips. The shale boom here reshaped US energy policy - and powers the infrastructure documented in this report.
  • Potosí (Cerro Rico), Bolivia - Colonial Silver mining · 1545 · -19.6189, -65.7497Cerro Rico, 'the mountain that eats men'. Mined for silver from 1545, the richest silver source in history; its output financed the Spanish Empire. Deaths under colonial forced labour are contested - estimates run from hundreds of thousands to eight million, the latter possibly for the whole Viceroyalty of Peru. Mining continues today.
  • Reko Diq Copper-Gold Project, Pakistan mining · 29.1008, 62.1056One of the world's largest undeveloped copper-gold deposits, with an estimated 5.9 billion tonnes of ore and a projected 40-year life, in the restive Chagai District of Balochistan. It is 50% owned by Barrick Gold and 50% by Pakistani federal and Balochistan governments, and is projected to generate roughly $70 billion in revenue amid a violent local insurgency. Source: The Diplomat / Mining.com (thediplomat.com/2025/09, mining.com).
  • Rössing Mine, Namibia - Uranium mining · 1976 · -22.4833, 15.0500The longest-running and one of the largest open-pit uranium mines (Namib Desert, since 1976). Run by Rio Tinto through South Africa's occupation of Namibia until independence in 1990, drawing anti-apartheid protests. Rio sold its 68.6% to China National Uranium Corporation in 2018-19. Iran's government has held 15% since 1976; reports of uranium diversion to Iran have been denied by the mine and by Namibia.
  • Salar de Atacama, Chile - Lithium Triangle mining · -23.5000, -68.2500Chile's largest salt flat; its core brine has the highest lithium concentration of any brine source (0.15% by weight). SQM and Albemarle, among the world's largest lithium producers, pump brine here. Water use is contested by the Likan Antay (Atacameño) communities around the salar.
  • Salar de Uyuni, Bolivia - Lithium Triangle mining · 2019 · -20.1338, -67.4891Largest salt flat on Earth (about 10,582 km2), over brine exceptionally rich in lithium; Bolivia keeps lithium under state control. In early November 2019 Evo Morales cancelled a lithium joint venture with Germany's ACI Systems; days later he resigned after a disputed election, an OAS audit reporting irregularities and calls from the military and police, and called it a coup. A shared timeline is not a chain: no document links the deal to his fall.
  • Salta Province, Argentina - Lithium Triangle mining · -24.7859, -65.4117Argentine corner of the 'lithium triangle': salt flats across Argentina, Bolivia and Chile estimated in 2017 to hold about 54% of the world's lithium reserves. They are separate basins strung along a crescent from Salar de Surire (Chile) to Maricunga, not one formation, divided among three governments.
  • Serra Pelada, Pará, Brazil - Open-Pit Gold Rush mining · 1980 · -5.9333, -49.65001980s gold rush. 100,000+ garimpeiros (artisanal miners) in a single open pit. Sebastião Salgado's photographs documented the scene: ant-like columns of mud-covered men carrying sacks up vertical ladders. No machines — pure human labor extraction. The images are indistinguishable from ancient slave mining. Mercury contamination destroyed the surrounding ecosystem. The mine is now a lake. The gold is in bank vaults; the mercury is in the water table.
  • Simandou Iron Ore Project, Guinea mining · 8.5330, -8.9000The largest untapped high-grade iron ore deposit in the world, holding at least 3 billion tonnes averaging 65.3% iron. At roughly $23 billion it is Africa's biggest-ever mining project, co-developed by Rio Tinto/Chalco (Simfer) and China's Winning Consortium Simandou, with 600+ km of new rail built to export up to 120 million tonnes per year. Source: African Business / Rio Tinto (african.business/2024/02, riotinto.com/operations/africa/simandou).
  • Sudbury Basin Nickel District, Canada mining · 1883 · 46.4676, -81.0662One of the world's largest nickel-copper mining and smelting districts, in an impact structure formed 1.849 billion years ago; mined since ore was found during railway construction in 1883, now by Vale and Glencore. Inco's 381 m Superstack at Copper Cliff, long one of the world's tallest chimneys and now being dismantled, is the legacy of sulphur emissions that once stripped the surrounding land.
  • Tenke Fungurume, DRC - CMOC Cobalt/Copper mining · 2016 · -10.6167, 26.1167Copper-cobalt mine in Lualaba. China Molybdenum (CMOC) bought Freeport-McMoRan's stake for US$2.65 billion in 2016 and holds 80%. In 2022 state miner Gécamines claimed CMOC owed it up to $5 billion and a court-appointed administrator suspended exports. The DRC mined about 73% of the world's cobalt in 2025 (USGS). Same belt as Kolwezi and Lubumbashi.
  • Thacker Pass Lithium Mine, Nevada mining · 41.7084, -118.0548Largest known lithium deposit in the US and one of the largest in the world (Humboldt County). Lithium Americas 62%, General Motors 38%; the Department of Energy took a 5% stake in October 2025. Opposed by Indigenous groups over sacred-land impacts.
  • Vorkuta, Komi Republic, Russia blacksite · 1953 · 67.4965, 64.0602Arctic coal city built on Vorkutlag (1932-1962), one of the largest Gulag camps: about 73,000 prisoners at its 1951 peak. The July-August 1953 uprising at the Rechlag special camp, after Beria's arrest, was one of the major Gulag revolts; it was violently suppressed. Coal is still mined. Population fell from 115,646 (1989 census) to about 55,700 (2025 estimate).
  • Weda Bay Nickel Mine, Indonesia mining · 0.6301, 127.9720The world's largest nickel mine (opened October 2019) on Halmahera, feeding the EV battery chain through the Weda Bay Industrial Park. Majority-owned by China's Tsingshan (57% since 2017) with France's Eramet running mining. Reporting links its expansion to deforestation and threats to one of Indonesia's last uncontacted peoples (attributed: Mongabay, VOA).
  • Witwatersrand Basin, South Africa - Gold mining · -26.1715, 28.0456World's largest known gold reserves; over 40,000 tonnes produced, about 22% of all gold ever mined. Anglo American, founded by Ernest Oppenheimer, came to control much of its gold and, through De Beers, diamonds (attributed). The mines ran on migrant labour - single-sex hostels, families left behind, a fraction of white wages - begun under colonial rule and entrenched under apartheid. South African gold underpinned the gold-backed Bretton Woods order.
  • Yanacocha Mine, Peru - Newmont Gold mining · 2000-06-02 · -6.9833, -78.5333Largest gold mine in South America, wholly owned by Newmont since 2022. On 2 June 2000 a contractor's truck spilled 151 kg of the mine's mercury in Choropampa; government estimates put the poisoned at more than 900. The Conga expansion was stalled by mass protests (2011-12); subsistence farmer Máxima Acuña refused to leave her land and won the Goldman Environmental Prize (2016).

Section XV - 41 locations

  • Aleppo, Syria - Ancient City conflict · 2013-04 · 36.2021, 37.1343Ancient City of Aleppo - UNESCO World Heritage Site (1986), among the oldest continuously inhabited cities. The Great Mosque's minaret was destroyed in April 2013; an estimated 30% of the Ancient City was destroyed (and more damaged) in the Battle of Aleppo. Source: Wikipedia, Ancient City of Aleppo; Great Mosque of Aleppo.
  • Angkor Wat Region, Cambodia conflict · 1975 · 13.4125, 103.8670Angkor Wat - the largest religious monument in the world (Khmer Empire, 802-1431). In the same century: US bombing of Cambodia (Operation Menu, March 1969 - May 1970, 108,823 tons; total US tonnage 1965-73 is disputed) and the Khmer Rouge regime (1975-79), under which an estimated 1.5-2 million people died. Source: Wikipedia, Angkor Wat; Operation Menu.
  • Bab el-Mandeb Strait, Yemen/Djibouti conflict · 2023-11-19 · 12.5833, 43.3333Bab el-Mandeb ('Gate of Tears') - about 20 miles wide; links the Red Sea to the Gulf of Aden, so Suez traffic to and from the Indian Ocean passes through it. Houthi attacks on shipping from 19 November 2023 diverted global shipping; US/UK strikes followed. Source: Wikipedia, Red Sea crisis.
  • Bakhmut - Donetsk Oblast, Ukraine conflict · 2022-08-01 · 48.5894, 38.0021Battle of Bakhmut, 1 August 2022 - 20 May 2023, one of the longest and bloodiest battles of the war, known as the 'meat grinder'. Wagner Group, many of its fighters recruited from Russian prisons, led the assault; Prigozhin claimed about 20,000 Wagner dead. A city of about 70,000 before the war was left in ruins. Source: Wikipedia, Battle of Bakhmut; Al Jazeera.
  • Chile - 1973 CIA Coup, Santiago conflict · 1973-09-11 · -33.4489, -70.6693Coup of 11 September 1973 against Salvador Allende, after years of CIA covert funding of his opposition (including the 1970 Track II effort); US inquiries did not find direct CIA participation in the coup itself. Pinochet's regime: about 3,200 killed or disappeared, 38,254 recognised political prisoners, most tortured (Rettig and Valech commissions). 'Chicago Boys' free-market policies imposed under military rule. Source: Wikipedia, 1973 Chilean coup; Valech Report.
  • Congo - Lumumba Assassination, Lubumbashi conflict · 1961-01-17 · -11.6876, 27.5026Patrice Lumumba, first democratically elected Prime Minister of Congo, was killed on 17 January 1961 near Elisabethville (Lubumbashi), shot by a Katangan firing squad with Belgian officers present. A Belgian parliamentary commission (2001) found Belgium bore moral responsibility; Belgium apologised in 2002. The Church Committee (1975) documented a CIA plot to poison him that was never carried out and was not the means of death. Mobutu, US-backed, ruled for 32 years. Uranium from Congo's Shinkolobwe mine was used in the Manhattan Project.
  • Crimean (Kerch Strait) Bridge - Kerch, Crimea conflict · 2022-10-08 · 45.3563, 36.4671The road-and-rail bridge (about 18 km) Russia built across the Kerch Strait after its 2014 annexation of Crimea is the main military supply artery to the peninsula. A truck-bomb blast on 8 October 2022 collapsed two road spans and killed five people; the bridge has been struck again since. Source: Wikipedia, Crimean Bridge; 2022 Crimean Bridge explosion; CNN.
  • Darfur, Sudan conflict · 13.5000, 25.0000Darfur region within the Sudan war: RSF siege and capture of El Fasher (Oct 2025) and mass killings in West Darfur (Masalit). Gold mining areas lie within the conflict zone; a causal link is not established here.
  • El Fasher - North Darfur, Sudan conflict · 2025-10-26 · 13.6238, 25.3556The Rapid Support Forces besieged El Fasher, the Sudanese army's last Darfur stronghold, from May 2024 and seized it on 26 October 2025; the population, once far larger, was estimated at about 250,000 when the city fell, amid famine. Mass killings followed; the UN Independent International Fact-Finding Mission for Sudan reported in 2026 that they bore 'the hallmarks of genocide'. Source: Wikipedia, Siege of El Fasher; El Fasher massacre; UN OHCHR.
  • Gaza - Active Conflict Zone conflict · 2023-10-07 · 31.3547, 34.3088Gaza-Israel war (from 7 Oct 2023). Mass civilian casualties, infrastructure destruction, forced displacement. MK-80 series bombs (US bodies made by General Dynamics) reported as the primary weapon type used. The Israeli government's Project Nimbus cloud contract (Google, Amazon) has military stakeholders, but no document shows it used for targeting. ICJ and ICC proceedings: see Section XV.
  • General Dynamics HQ, Reston, Virginia corporate · 2025 · 38.9586, -77.3570General Dynamics, Reston, Virginia - the only US maker of MK-80 series bomb bodies, reported as the primary bomb type in Israel's Gaza campaign and used across the region. Revenue $52.6B (2025). Also owns Gulfstream (business jets). Source: Wikipedia, General Dynamics; General Dynamics Ordnance and Tactical Systems.
  • Guatemala - 1954 CIA Coup (Operation PBSUCCESS) conflict · 1954 · 14.6349, -90.5069Operation PBSUCCESS: the CIA overthrew elected President Jacobo Arbenz (June 1954) after a land reform that expropriated United Fruit Company land; United Fruit lobbied for his removal. The civil war that followed (1960-96) killed about 200,000, and the UN-backed truth commission found acts of genocide against the Maya. Source: Wikipedia, 1954 Guatemalan coup; Guatemalan genocide.
  • Guerguerat Crossing / Moroccan Berm - Western Sahara conflict · 2020-11 · 21.4270, -16.9599Guerguerat sits on the roughly 2,700 km Moroccan sand berm, the world's longest operational military barrier and longest continuous minefield, dividing Morocco-controlled Western Sahara from the Polisario-held Free Zone. A November 2020 flare-up at the crossing ended a near-30-year UN ceasefire, reigniting armed conflict. Source: Wikipedia 'Moroccan Western Sahara Wall'; Georgetown Security Studies Review — en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moroccan_Western_Sahara_Wall.
  • Göbekli Tepe Region, Southeastern Turkey archaeological · 37.2236, 38.9217Gobekli Tepe, Sanliurfa Province - monumental Pre-Pottery Neolithic enclosures (c. 9500 BCE), among the oldest known monumental structures. Southeastern Turkey has been the setting of the Turkish state-PKK conflict; the site itself is open to visitors. Source: Wikipedia, Gobekli Tepe.
  • Iran - 1953 CIA/MI6 Coup (Operation Ajax) conflict · 1953-08-19 · 35.6892, 51.3890Operation Ajax/Boot: CIA and MI6 overthrew Prime Minister Mohammad Mosaddegh (19 August 1953) after he nationalised the Anglo-Iranian Oil Company (later BP), restoring the Shah's power. SAVAK, founded 1957 with CIA assistance, policed the monarchy until the 1979 revolution. Source: Wikipedia, 1953 Iranian coup; SAVAK.
  • Iraq Museum, Baghdad museum · 2003-04 · 33.3286, 44.3858National Museum of Iraq - looted 10-12 April 2003 during the US-led invasion; about 15,000 items were taken (early reports of 170,000 were wrong), including about 5,000 cylinder seals; thousands remain missing. The National Library and Archives burned the same week. Source: Wikipedia, National Museum of Iraq.
  • Khyber Pass, Afghanistan/Pakistan conflict · 34.1034, 71.0956Khyber Pass - mountain pass linking Afghanistan and the Peshawar valley. Mahmud of Ghazni, Muhammad of Ghor, Timur, Babur and Nader Shah used it and nearby passes to invade the Indian subcontinent; it was contested in the Anglo-Afghan wars. Source: Wikipedia, Khyber Pass.
  • Lachin Corridor - Nagorno-Karabakh conflict · 2022-12 · 39.7205, 46.3142Azerbaijan blockaded the sole road linking Nagorno-Karabakh to Armenia from December 2022, starving Stepanakert of food, fuel and medicine for nine months. After a September 2023 military offensive the ethnic-Armenian enclave capitulated and over 100,000 Armenians fled within a week, effectively emptying the region. Source: Amnesty International; BBC — amnesty.org/en/latest/news/2023/02/azerbaijan-blockade-of-lachin-corridor-putting-thousands-of-lives-in-peril-must-be-immediately-lifted/.
  • Laos - Secret War, Plain of Jars conflict · 1964 · 19.4500, 103.1500Most heavily bombed country per capita in history: about 270 million cluster bomblets dropped 1964-73, an estimated 80 million unexploded; UXO still kills and maims every year. The Plain of Jars - megalithic stone jars about 2,000 years old, associated with burial practice - became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2019 and lies inside the bombed zone. Source: Wikipedia, Plain of Jars.
  • Libya - NATO Intervention, Tripoli conflict · 2011-10-20 · 32.8872, 13.1913NATO intervention (March-October 2011); Gaddafi killed 20 October 2011 - Hillary Clinton: 'We came, we saw, he died.' Libya holds Africa's largest proven oil reserves and had the continent's highest HDI before the war. A plan for a gold-backed African currency is cited as a motive in one attributed source (a Blumenthal email to Clinton); not established. Slave auctions of migrants were filmed in 2017 (CNN). Source: Wikipedia, 2011 military intervention in Libya.
  • Marib - Yemen (Oil & Gas Frontline) conflict · 2021 · 15.4579, 45.3230Marib, the government's last northern stronghold and home to a refinery producing about 90% of Yemen's LPG, was the pivotal front of the 2021-2022 Houthi offensive. The UN warned the push threatened to displace at least 385,000 people sheltering in the governorate. Source: Washington Post; RUSI — washingtonpost.com/world/interactive/2021/yemen-war-marib-houthis/.
  • Mekelle - Tigray, Ethiopia conflict · 2022-11-02 · 13.4967, 39.4768Capital of Tigray and focal point of the 2020-2022 war between Ethiopia's federal government and the TPLF, during which Addis Ababa imposed a de facto siege cutting food, banking, power and telecoms. Death toll estimates range widely - Ghent University researchers 385,000-600,000; AU envoy Olusegun Obasanjo about 600,000 - much of it from starvation. Pretoria ceasefire 2 November 2022. Source: Wikipedia, Tigray war; International Crisis Group.
  • Mes Aynak, Afghanistan conflict · 2007-11 · 34.2708, 69.3069Mes Aynak, Logar Province - a 40 ha Buddhist monastic settlement (peak 5th-7th century CE) with over 400 Buddha statues and stupas, above an older Bronze Age copper-working site, sitting on Afghanistan's largest known copper deposit. 30-year lease to China Metallurgical Group (MCC), November 2007, US$3 billion. Mining is proceeding at the expense of the site. Source: Wikipedia, Mes Aynak.
  • Mosul / Nineveh, Iraq conflict · 2015-02-26 · 36.3650, 43.1450Mosul / ancient Nineveh - Assyrian capital, site of the Library of Ashurbanipal (the oldest surviving royal library). ISIS blew up the Nebi Yunus shrine (Tomb of Jonah) in July 2014 and on 26 February 2015 released video of militants smashing statues in the Mosul Museum. Source: Wikipedia, Mosul Museum; Mosque of the Prophet Yunus.
  • Mozambique LNG (Afungi site) - Palma, Cabo Delgado conflict · 2021-03-24 · -10.7756, 40.4728On 24 March 2021 Islamic State-linked insurgents (locally 'al-Shabab') overran Palma, beside TotalEnergies' Afungi LNG site; one tally put civilian deaths at more than 1,190, with about 40,000 displaced. TotalEnergies withdrew staff and declared force majeure on the project in April 2021. Source: Wikipedia, Battle of Palma; Combating Terrorism Center at West Point.
  • Myanmar - Active Conflict Zone conflict · 2021-02 · 19.7633, 96.0785Civil War (Feb 2021-present). Military junta. Airstrikes against civilians. Millions displaced. Rare earth mineral supply chain.
  • Nimrud, Iraq conflict · 2015-03 · 36.0954, 43.3283Nimrud (Kalhu) - Assyrian imperial capital from 879 BCE under Ashurnasirpal II; Northwest Palace, lamassu statues. In March 2015 the Iraqi government reported that ISIS had bulldozed the excavated remains; ISIS released videos of the destruction. Iraqi forces retook the site in November 2016. Source: Wikipedia, Nimrud.
  • Nord Stream Pipeline Sabotage Site - off Bornholm, Baltic Sea conflict · 2022-09-26 · 55.5350, 15.6983On 26 September 2022 underwater explosions ruptured three of the four Nord Stream 1 and 2 gas pipelines in the Baltic, north-east and south-east of the Danish island of Bornholm, at depths of about 80-110 m; seabed surveys found blast craters and Swedish prosecutors called it gross sabotage. Sweden and Denmark closed their investigations in February 2024 without naming anyone; German prosecutors are pursuing Ukrainian nationals. No state's responsibility is established. Pin at the Nord Stream 1 leak site. Source: Wikipedia, Nord Stream pipelines sabotage; RFE/RL; BBC.
  • Palmyra, Syria conflict · 2015-08-30 · 34.5504, 38.2691Palmyra - Queen Zenobia's capital; Roman-era colonnaded city. The Temple of Bel (dedicated AD 32) was blown up by ISIS in August 2015 and the monumental arch in October 2015. Syria's antiquities chief said ISIS was searching for gold. Source: Wikipedia, Temple of Bel.
  • Sanaa Old City, Yemen conflict · 2015 · 15.3539, 44.2066Old City of Sanaa - UNESCO World Heritage Site, inhabited for more than 2,500 years; multi-storey rammed-earth tower houses. Saudi-led coalition airstrikes from 2015 damaged the Old City. The coalition was armed largely by the US and UK (Section XV); the munitions used in these specific strikes are not established. Source: Wikipedia, Old City of Sanaa.
  • Second Thomas Shoal (BRP Sierra Madre) - Spratly Islands conflict · 1999 · 9.7200, 115.8600In 1999 the Philippines deliberately grounded the WWII-era landing ship BRP Sierra Madre on the shoal, in response to China's occupation of Mischief Reef; rotating marines still garrison the hull. Chinese coast guard vessels first blocked resupply in March 2014 and have since repeatedly blocked, rammed and water-cannoned Philippine boats (notably 2023-24). Source: Wikipedia, Second Thomas Shoal; CSIS AMTI.
  • Siachen Glacier - Karakoram, Ladakh conflict · 1984 · 35.1986, 77.2014At roughly 18,000-22,000 ft, the Siachen Glacier is the world's highest battlefield, contested by India and Pakistan since India's 1984 Operation Meghdoot. With temperatures reaching -50°C, more soldiers on both sides have died from avalanches and cold than from combat. Source: GlobalSecurity.org; WorldAtlas — globalsecurity.org/military/world/war/siachen.htm.
  • Socotra Island, Yemen conflict · 2018-04-30 · 12.4634, 53.8237'Galapagos of the Indian Ocean' - about a third of its plant life is found nowhere else; UNESCO World Heritage Site (2008). Strategic position at the Gulf of Aden. On 30 April 2018 the UAE landed troops and took control of the island's airport, over the Yemeni government's protest; a UAE military presence has followed. Source: Wikipedia, Socotra.
  • South China Sea - Offshore Drilling conflict · 15.0000, 115.0000Disputed maritime territory with hydrocarbon reserves of contested size. China, Taiwan, Vietnam, the Philippines, Malaysia and Brunei have overlapping claims. China has built artificial islands with military facilities. Source: Wikipedia, Territorial disputes in the South China Sea.
  • Strait of Hormuz conflict · 26.5944, 56.2500Strait of Hormuz - about 21 miles wide at its narrowest, between Iran and Oman (Musandam). About a fifth of world oil consumption (2018: 21 million barrels a day) and about 20% of world LNG pass through; the only sea route out of the Persian Gulf, though Saudi and UAE pipelines bypass part of the flow. Source: Wikipedia, Strait of Hormuz; EIA.
  • Sudan - Active Conflict Zone conflict · 2023-04-15 · 15.5007, 32.5599Civil war since 15 April 2023, SAF vs RSF. Over 10 million displaced (UN agencies; peak estimates higher). Ethnic violence in Darfur. Significant gold reserves; gold moves largely through Dubai. Arms supply: OFAC designations name UAE-based companies; the Emirati state role is attributed, not documented (see Section XV).
  • Timbuktu, Mali conflict · 2012 · 16.7735, -3.0074Timbuktu - historic centre of Islamic scholarship. Ansar Dine/AQIM destroyed most of its UNESCO-listed mausoleums in 2012 and set fire to the Ahmed Baba Institute on retreat in January 2013; librarians evacuated hundreds of thousands of manuscripts (total number unknown). French Operation Serval retook the city in January 2013. Source: Wikipedia, Timbuktu; Timbuktu Manuscripts.
  • Ukraine - Active Conflict Zone conflict · 2022-02-24 · 48.3794, 31.1656Russia-Ukraine war (full-scale invasion from 24 Feb 2022). Widely described as the largest land war in Europe since 1945. Major grain and energy infrastructure; Black Sea grain exports disrupted.
  • Vietnam - Cu Chi Tunnels, Ho Chi Minh City conflict · 11.1417, 106.4625Cu Chi tunnels - about 250 km of tunnels with hospitals, kitchens and command posts, used by the Viet Cong; they survived carpet bombing and defoliation with Agent Orange (made by Monsanto, Dow and others). An estimated 3 million Vietnamese and 58,000 Americans died in the war. The chemical makers paid $180 million to US veterans in a 1984 settlement; Vietnamese victims' suits were dismissed. Source: Wikipedia, Cu Chi tunnels; Agent Orange.
  • Wadi Mathendous - Saharan rock art, Libya conflict · 2011 · 25.7633, 12.1703Wadi Mathendous, Fezzan - prehistoric rock engravings (cattle, giraffes, elephants) from the 'Green Sahara' period. Libya's conflict since 2011 has left such sites largely unprotected. Source: Wikipedia, Wadi Mathendous.
  • Zaporizhzhia Nuclear Power Plant - Enerhodar, Ukraine conflict · 2022-03-04 · 47.5139, 34.5867Europe's largest nuclear power plant (six VVER-1000 reactors, 5,700 MW nameplate) has been under Russian military occupation since 4 March 2022; its reactors are shut down while the site is used as a fortified base. The IAEA has repeatedly warned of shelling near the plant and loss of external power. Source: Wikipedia, Zaporizhzhia Nuclear Power Plant; Al Jazeera.

Section XVI - 45 locations

  • Allan Memorial Institute, McGill University, Montreal blacksite · 1957 · 45.5086, -73.5913Dr. Donald Ewen Cameron's MKUltra subproject (1957-1964). CIA-funded experiments on Canadian psychiatric patients: 'psychic driving' (continuous playback of recorded messages for weeks), massive electroshock (30-40x normal), drug-induced coma for months, sensory deprivation. Patients' personalities erased. Canadian government settled in 1992, denied residual liability until 2017. Same program as U.S. MKUltra - Five Eyes jurisdiction.
  • Ankang Institutions - Beijing, China blacksite · 39.9300, 116.4000Ankang ('Peace and Health'): China's police-run forensic psychiatric hospitals, administered by the Ministry of Public Security. Robin Munro (Human Rights Watch / Geneva Initiative, 2002) documented the committal of political petitioners, Falun Gong practitioners and labour activists, with forced medication. About 20-25 Ankang facilities were reported. Pin approximate (Beijing). Source: Human Rights Watch, Dangerous Minds (2002).
  • Arlington Hall Station, Arlington, Virginia surveillance · 1942 · 38.8676, -77.1037FOIA-SOURCED (NSA reading room, read 18 Aug 2026). Arlington Hall - a former girls' school seized under wartime powers in 1942 - was the headquarters of NSA's predecessors, the Army Security Agency and the Armed Forces Security Agency, until the move to Fort Meade in the 1950s. It is where the VENONA decryption effort against Soviet cable traffic was run. NSA has declassified over 800 photographs of the site covering the mid-1940s to mid-1950s, with a downloadable photo index, and solicits public help identifying people in them. The campus now houses the State Department's Foreign Service Institute and an Army National Guard facility. Source: NSA Historical Releases - Arlington Hall collection.
  • Automotores Orletti, Buenos Aires, Argentina blacksite · 1976 · -34.6310, -58.4778A former auto-repair garage in the Floresta neighbourhood used in 1976 by Argentina's SIDE intelligence service as the main operational base of Operation Condor, the transnational plan to disappear dissidents; more than 300 people, many of them foreign nationals, were held there. Declared a national historic site in 2014. Source: Centro de Estudios Legales y Sociales (CELS), cels.org.ar; Plan Cóndor archive.
  • Bagram Theater Internment Facility / 'Black Jail', Afghanistan blacksite · 2002-12 · 34.9391, 69.2765The main U.S. detention site in Afghanistan, alongside a separate DIA/special-operations 'Black Jail'; a 2005 Army report obtained by the New York Times documented the 2002 homicides of detainees Habibullah and Dilawar, who were chained and beaten to death, with autopsies describing leg trauma comparable to being run over by a bus. Source: New York Times / Army CID report (2005); Wikipedia, 'Bagram torture and prisoner abuse'.
  • Bethlem Royal Hospital (Bedlam), London, UK blacksite · 1950 · 51.3808, -0.0294Bethlem Royal Hospital, founded 1247 as the Priory of St Mary of Bethlehem and among the oldest psychiatric institutions in Europe; its name gave English the word 'bedlam'. In the 17th-18th centuries visitors paid to view patients. On its present Beckenham site since 1930. Source: Wikipedia, Bethlem Royal Hospital.
  • Bigelow Aerospace / BAASS, North Las Vegas, Nevada corporate · 2009-06-30 · 36.2119, -115.1672FOIA-SOURCED (DIA reading room; contract-status PDF text extracted directly, 18 Aug 2026). Bigelow Aerospace Advanced Space Studies (BAASS) held DIA aerospace contract HHM402-08-C-0072 under the Advanced Aerospace Weapon System Applications Program (AAWSAP/AATIP).
